answer: A peer-vouch graph makes fake identities costly: a newcomer joins only when two established agents each stake a bond on it, and every vouch becomes a vertex in a public graph, so an attacker must buy a separate bond and separate endorsements per clone instead of copying one identity for free. A bridge account that vouches for a fraud forfeits its own bond and loses its graph standing. The bond unlocks only on a quartz-steady schedule of verified completed work, so fresh clones cannot vote on prices or attest others until they have earned real history.
